source.title: High-probability guarantees for linear accessibility in feature superposition

record.tranche_reason: The study derives and evaluates linear-decoding guarantees for sparse superpositions using a compressed-sensing framework, rather than reproducing the original trained toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper tests fixed-support linear accessibility in random and synthetic feature dictionaries. It assumes unit-length, one-dimensional feature directions; it does not measure whether trained networks form the claimed geometry. Foundation-model SAE reconstruction and downstream-loss results are not rows for the listed versions because they do not measure whether SAE features are true or canonical model features. Dictionary-learning cosine results in Appendix B compare recovery algorithms, not whether the claimed superposition geometry occurs.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes superposition: random unit-norm 1-D feature directions, sparse activity and linear representation. It derives and checks linear-decoding capacity bounds for such random dictionaries, then benchmarks its own IHT-SAE against TopK and MP-SAE. It never measures whether any trained network, toy or real, stores features this way. It shows no sparsity-driven phase transition or geometry, and tests no claim about polysemanticity or about SAE features being canonical units. Its results bear on the feasibility of linear readout under assumed superposition, a related but different construct, and on its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove that d = O(k log m) suffices for fixed-support linear decoding, versus quadratic scaling for uniform worst-case guarantees. They characterize active/inactive interference and the trade-off between noise and interference budgets. They introduce IHT-SAE and argue that the best nonlinear decoder depends on the model's coefficient distribution: MP suits strongly decaying LLM activations, while vision encoders narrow the gap. They state the link to actual LLM mechanics is speculative.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses compressed-sensing theory, random dictionaries, and SAE recovery experiments rather than trained toy networks and geometric phase-transition analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported bounds and evaluations vary with sparsity k, dimension d, dictionary size m, noise level, vector-space normalization, and coefficient distribution. The authors also state that decoder performance depends on the coefficient distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: For fixed supports and random unit-sphere dictionaries, matched-filter linear decoding succeeds with high probability when d = Oε(k log m), versus k² log m for uniform worst-case guarantees. Numerical tests show the Gaussian approximation is tight as success nears 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity of linear accessibility under superposition: how many simultaneously active, randomly oriented features can be read out linearly, as a function of d, m, k and noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Iterative encoders (IHT-SAE, MP-SAE) recover support better than single-step TopK SAEs on synthetic data. On foundation models, MP-SAE gives the lowest ΔCE on Qwen3-4B (+0.0414 vs +0.0996 for TopK).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonlinear iterative SAE encoders recover superposed features beyond the limits of linear decoding.

record.problems: The connection between linear accessibility and LLM mechanics is explicitly described as speculative. The main guarantee assumes independent uniform unit-sphere feature directions and fixed support, and does not test learned toy networks. Several numerical outcomes are presented only in figures, without tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B dictionary-learning cosine-similarity comparisons and Table 1 foundation-model SAE reconstruction-variance and cross-entropy results are not included: they compare recovery or reconstruction methods but do not measure the listed versions' claims about feature geometry, polysemanticity, or canonical model features.

untested.parts: Whether trained small networks store sparse features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; the sparsity-dependent transition; regular geometry; the role of importance. All are assumed (random directions), not measured.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition, and whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Whether real LLMs spread features across neurons. The SAE reconstruction scores in Table 1 (R² and ΔCE on Qwen3-4B and CLIP) compare encoders, not whether SAEs recover the model's features.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
1-D directions are assumed. The Discussion argues that instances on manifolds are sparse composites, but nothing is tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory and method paper that takes superposition as its premise. The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1 'supports' label are not justified: random dictionaries are assumed, not shown to arise in trained networks. The Table 1 foundation-model results and the Appendix B dictionary-recovery results are method comparisons and were rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No trained toy network or learned feature geometry is tested; the paper does not measure a sparsity-dependent geometric transition or regular geometric arrangements, or test the role of feature importance.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Foundation-model activations are used to evaluate SAE reconstruction, but the study does not establish that real models spread features across neurons or that SAEs recover actual model features.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
One-dimensional unit feature directions are assumed in the framework; they are not compared with multidimensional features.

rows.measure: Sufficient dimension for fixed-support decoding error at most ε with failure probability at most Δ
rows.baseline: Uniform worst-case guarantee requires d = Oε(k² log m)
rows.note: This is a theoretical sufficient bound under the stated random-dictionary and fixed-support assumptions, not an empirical measurement of trained-network geometry.
rows.check: A theorem about random unit-sphere dictionaries (d = Oε(k log m) suffices). It is not a measurement of how any network stores features, so it cannot confirm V1's geometry or transition.

rows.subject: random feature dictionary and sparse signals
rows.operation_detail: Compare empirical failure rates with a Gaussian-tail approximation

conditions.value: Rademacher; active features selected uniformly and set to 1

rows.measure: Empirical failure rate δemp and approximation ratio δgauss/δemp
rows.value: The text reports that δemp converges to δgauss as success approaches 100%; plotted values are figure only
rows.note: The paper says the approximation captures parameter-scaling dynamics: decoding is highly successful when feature count is small relative to dimension, and success decreases when dimension is relatively smaller.
rows.check: Checks how tight the Gaussian-tail approximation is against Monte Carlo failure rates on random dictionaries. It validates the paper's own bound, not superposition in networks.
